raw_response:
I'm 69 this year. Fifty years I've been on this land, never spent a day in school, but I know what I'm doing. Me and the old lady — just the two of us now, both getting old — we farm 57 mu out in Quzhou. Our boy works construction in Shijiazhuang, sends money sometimes, but I don't plan on it. What I have is what I have.

Fifty mu is wheat-maize, same rotation I've done forever. Seven mu by the east road I keep for scallions — that's my cash crop, though my back hates me for it.

The wheat went in last October, early, before National Day. Used my own seed, saved from the year before. No need to pay for seed when your own grows fine. At planting I put down one full bag of compound fertilizer per mu — the 50-jin bag, same as my father did and his father before him. Now it's April, wheat is up to my knee and turning a bit yellow. Time to topdress. I put half a bag of urea on each mu, about 25 jin. I learned my lesson three years ago when I put a whole extra bag on five mu and it all flattened in the wind. Lost half the yield on that patch. Better a bit less than too much. I'll irrigate three times for the wheat — once now to wash the urea in, once at heading in May, and once more in early June if it's dry before harvest. Each time costs me diesel for the pump, about 20 yuan per mu, so I watch the sky. If heaven sends rain, I save the money.

Maize goes in right after wheat comes off, mid-June. No rest — sometimes only five or six days between. I buy hybrid seed new every year, 60 yuan a bag, one bag covers three mu. I hire the custom planter from the village, 25 yuan per mu, because me and the old lady can't plant 50 mu by hand anymore. I put half a bag of compound fertilizer in the furrow at planting, and when the corn is knee-high — about 20 days after — I topdress with half a bag of urea per mu. That's it. Maize doesn't need fussing like wheat. Irrigate once at the big trumpet leaf stage, maybe twice if August turns hot and dry. Last two summers were wet enough, I only pumped once. Saved good money.

Scallions — I planted them in March, seven mu. Those need work. I put two cartloads of chicken manure per mu at planting, bought from Old Wang's chicken farm down the road, 80 yuan a cart. Plus half a bag of compound. Then I hill them up three times, and that's where the labor goes. Me and the old lady can't do all that bending and hoeing anymore. I hire Auntie Li and Auntie Zhang from the village, 80 yuan a day each. They work about 12 days each across the season for the hilling and weeding. I topdress the scallions once more with urea at the second hilling, about 15 jin per mu. Irrigate twice, carefully — not too much or they rot at the root.

For spraying — wheat gets herbicide in spring if I see too many weeds, and I watch for aphids. Maize gets herbicide at planting. Scallions need fungicide, they get leaf blight when the weather turns wet.

Money this year — I got about 28,000 yuan I can spend on the fields. That's everything. Fertilizer is the big bite, then diesel for water, then labor for the scallions. I keep 3,000 yuan in the tin box under the bed for medicine. At our age, you don't gamble everything.

Yields? Wheat, I hope for 800 jin per mu — about 400 kg. If I get 850 jin I'll be happy. Maize, 900 jin per mu, about 450 kg. Scallions, if I hill them well and the price doesn't crash, 5,000 jin per mu — that's 2,500 kg. That's where I make my real money. Wheat and maize fill the belly; scallions fill the purse.
